The user wants a detailed technical essay of at least 800 words on paged key-value caches in transformer inference engines. This is a well-known topic — the PagedAttention approach popularized by vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023, "Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention"). I should cover:

1. Background: why KV caches exist, what they store, memory footprint
2. The problem with contiguous KV caches: fragmentation (internal and external), preemption, poor sharing, over-reservation
3. How paged KV caches work: blocks, block size, block tables, logical vs physical blocks, copy-on-write
4. Block tables: mapping logical positions to physical blocks, per-sequence metadata, how attention kernels use them (gather/scatter)
5. Eviction and memory management: allocation, freeing, reference counting, preemption and recomputation vs swapping, LRU eviction of cached blocks
6. Prefix sharing: copy-on-write, shared prefixes across sequences, system prompts, beam search, n-gram / multi-sampling, reference counts
7. Trade-offs vs contiguous cache: kernel complexity, non-coalesced memory access, block size choice, fragmentation elimination, throughput gains, latency overhead

**Background on speculative decoding:**

Autoregressive LLM inference is typically memory-bandwidth bound during decoding. Each token generation requires loading all model weights (or at least the active ones) from HBM into the compute units, but each token involves only a small amount of arithmetic per weight (one token's worth of activations). So arithmetic intensity (FLOPs per byte) is far below what modern GPUs can sustain; the GPU is mostly idle waiting on weight loads. Batch size 1 decoding is the classic case.
